items.text:
Belgium’s airports set to shut down due to anti-austerity strike
Skeyes halts air traffic control services, grounding flights at Belgian airports amid union-led strike.
Nearly all flights are set to be cancelled in Belgium on Monday after the country’s air traffic controller said its staff would take part in a national strike against government austerity measures.
Skeyes, the company responsible for Belgium’s air traffic control, said it would be unable to provide regular services at the country’s airports and in its airspace between 7am (06:00 GMT) and 9pm (20:00 GMT) on Monday.
“The anticipated staffing levels will not allow the safe handling of regular air traffic to be guaranteed during this period,” the company said. “Skeyes is therefore obliged to temporarily suspend the services concerned.”
It added that only essential services for emergencies and other safety-critical flights would continue.
The Brussels-Charleroi airport, a major European hub for low-cost airline Ryanair, said the strike would result in the “complete shutdown of all the country’s airports for an entire day”, affecting thousands of passengers.
“Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land,” the Brussels-Charleroi airport said, criticising a “last-minute decision” with “disastrous consequences”.
Brussels airport said most departing and arriving flights “will have to be cancelled”.
Pushback against austerity policies
Belgian unions have called for a nationwide day of action on Monday to protest against austerity and reform measures pursued by the country’s governing coalition.
The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which represents about 25 carriers, said the walkout would be the 11th strike affecting Belgian airspace in 11 months.
The unions also plan a large-scale demonstration in Brussels on Monday. Significant disruption is expected to public transport, while schools, government offices and refuse collection services may also be affected.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has been in protracted talks with his coalition partners on a cost-cutting budget that will save 10 billion euros ($11bn) over the next few years by Monday, in a bid to reduce the country’s high deficit.
Earlier in November, De Wever offered his resignation after his coalition failed to reach a deal. However, Belgium’s King Philippe rejected the resignation and gave the prime minister more time to find a solution.

items.text:
Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
- Published
A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed nine people, Ukrainian officials have said.
The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.
Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.
Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.
Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts.
In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.
Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.
Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".
Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".
Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".
The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.
In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.
Tkachenko previously said two other people were killed and eight wounded in the Vyshneve attack.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

items.text:
Indonesian police remove 24 body bags from factory fire site
Authorities in Java are searching for dozens of missing workers as they continue to battle remaining hotspots.
Indonesian authorities are set to resume the search for missing workers on Monday after police removed 24 body bags from a factory in Java gutted by a fire.
Firefighters continued to battle remaining hotspots on Sunday after the blaze broke out on Saturday evening at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, Serang regency, West Java province.
A search for dozens of missing workers was suspended overnight but would resume Monday morning, Hendra Kurniawan, the police chief of Indonesia’s Banten province, told local broadcaster Metro TV on Sunday.
Steven Erwin Wijaya, the CEO of the factory’s parent company, PT United Family Food, said at a news conference that about 300 people were present for Saturday’s shift, with 65 of them believed to have been in the affected area when the fire broke out.
In a statement that followed, the factory said 24 of the 65 workers had returned home, four were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained missing, and the whereabouts of another eight had yet to be confirmed.
At a news conference on Sunday, Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, a police disaster victim identification official, said the intensity of the fire had made it impossible to identify the recovered victims visually. She said they would collect DNA samples from relatives and the personal belongings of the missing workers, a process that could take two to three weeks.
The number of dead was not immediately clear. Police said that one body bag could contain parts of more than one person.
Authorities said the cause of the fire was being investigated. Parts of the building remained at risk of collapse, an official added.
Photos and videos circulating online on Sunday showed flames and thick smoke coming from the factory, which borders the capital, Jakarta. Footage from inside the three-storey building appeared to show the fire caused extensive damage, with equipment blackened and destroyed.
Indonesia has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.
A fire in an office building in Jakarta killed at least 22 people last December. An explosion at an Indonesian nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

items.title: US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
items.summary:
US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Trump’s comments were ‘entirely appropriate’ in the context of the summit.
United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify Preside
items.text:
US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Trump’s comments were ‘entirely appropriate’ in the context of the summit.
United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify President Donald Trump’s claims that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin is a “friend”.
In an appearance on the ABC News show This Week, journalist Jonathan Karl pressed Clayton on Trump’s recent remarks.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked.
Clayton responded by calling Trump’s meeting “historic” and his remarks “appropriate”, but the intelligence chief also clarified that the US has not taken Russia’s side when it comes to the country’s invasion of Ukraine.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said.
The scrutiny follows a first-ever confirmed meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.
The three world leaders had a roundtable on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen, China.
Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly praised Putin. In August 2025, Trump hosted the Russian leader in Alaska for Putin’s first visit to the US in nearly a decade.
Upon reuniting with Putin at the Shenzhen conference, Trump offered him a warm, light-hearted greeting.
“Who is he?” Trump joked, first pointing to Putin, then striding across the room to shake his hand. “He’s my friend.”
Trump has since doubled down on his remarks, posting several images of their meeting on social media, one of which bore the caption, “My Friend”.
When a reporter asked whether Russia was a “friend to America” in a news briefing on Friday, Trump brushed aside the question.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, proceeding to explain that he and Putin had grown close during an investigation into whether Russia had interfered in his favour during the 2016 US presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. And to be honest, he was very nice about it,” Trump explained.
The US State Department has long been critical of Russia over allegations of human rights abuses, including the torture and imprisonment of political dissidents.
Washington has also supported Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing billions in security assistance and weaponry.
Under Trump, however, that support has cooled, with the US president openly criticising his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for failing to cut a deal with Russia.
Such remarks have divided Republicans, with critics like outgoing US Representative Don Bacon accusing Trump of “playing footsie” with Putin.
“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and China,” Bacon said last week. “We stood for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values. President Trump has been terrible on this, right here.”
But in his television appearances on Sunday, Clayton defended Trump’s remarks, describing the president’s statements of friendship as “entirely appropriate” for building a personal rapport with the Russian leader.
He also praised Trump for uniting some of the world’s biggest powers for a conversation about nuclear proliferation.
“It should be assuring that you have the three world nuclear powers getting together and saying: We’re not going to go in that direction,” Clayton told This Week.
While the trilateral meeting concluded with a statement about “reducing nuclear risks”, critics point out no firm commitments were made.
Also on Sunday, in an appearance on CNN, Clayton reiterated his support for Trump’s remarks.
“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.

items.text:
Thousands rally in Istanbul against Turkey’s crackdown on opposition and media
Thousands marched in Istanbul on Sunday against a widening crackdown on Turkey’s opposition and independent media, days after police raided Sozcu TV and arrested senior staff. The main opposition Yeni Parti organised the protest after authorities installed a government-appointed trustee at the broadcaster, following similar moves against other independent outlets.
Several thousand people marched through Istanbul on Sunday to protest a growing crackdown on opposition and independent media outlets.
The protest was called by the main opposition Yeni Parti days after police raided Sozcu TV, installing a government-appointed trustee and arresting senior staff members.
It was the third such takeover in a year after similar moves against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel and leading digital news website T24.
Press freedom has come under sustained pressure over the past decade through prosecutions, digital censorship and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news", prompting criticism from rights groups at home and abroad.
Carrying a huge banner reading: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press and freedom for journalists," protesters marched through the Besiktas neighbourhood, chanting, cheering and whistling, an AFP journalist said.

As they reached the shores of the Bosphorus, several voiced concern at the narrowing space for voices perceived as critical of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his government.
"Our press has been silenced, all opposition channels have been silenced!" a 64-year-old protester called Tunay told AFPTV, without giving her surname.
"All our freedoms are on the verge of being restricted," she sighed. "As a country, we are very unhappy. We are anxious about the future."
The direction Turkey was heading in was "not good", agreed another demonstrator called Koksal, also 64.
"We are living through a period in which all democratic rights have disappeared," he told AFP.
"All democratic journalists and opposition television channels are being shut down, blacked out!" he explained, saying that he, like many others, were being forced to get their news from social media.
"But they are shutting down social media too, all forms of it that are effective."
Over the past two months, Turkey has arrested several journalists over their coverage of a multi-billion-dollar investment fund scandal, at least two of whom remain in pre-trial detention.
Twenty-five journalists are currently behind bars in Turkey, according to figures from the MLSA media rights group.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in
items.text:
‘Extremely concerning’: Inside a US Army plan to detonate Iowa lead stores
The US Army plans to invoke emergency powers to detonate 4 tonnes of lead azide in an Iowa town, despite a court-ordered stay.
The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in Iowa, defying a federal appeals court’s order suspending its permit to do so.
In a fact sheet this weekend, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said that two controlled explosions were scheduled for around noon (06:00 GMT) on Monday.
That announcement follows statements from the Department of Justice, arguing that Tuesday was the cut-off date to carry out a planned detonation.
Lead azide is a key explosive used in military ammunition. The Iowa stockpile has reportedly grown unstable, and Justice Department lawyers have warned that sub-freezing temperatures could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
“The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” their court filing said.
But critics have questioned the army’s rationale for pushing ahead with the planned detonation, despite the court order to pause it.
“Anyone can claim an emergency at any point and do whatever they want. I don’t think people can or should accept that,” said Thien Chau, a lawyer with the legal group Earthjustice, which represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
Chau told Al Jazeera that not enough has been done to mitigate the risk from the explosions, which are expected to release a cloud of lead into the air.
Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure, and the dense metal can cause birth defects, brain damage and infertility.
“Anyone who hears that the army plans to explode nearly 10,000 pounds [4,500kg] of [this chemical] would recognise that that is not normal,” Chau said.
“That is extraordinary, and that is not something that you just take lightly.”
An 11th-hour legal battle
The impending explosions come after a tense legal battle between the US government and environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council.
The groups have questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13. The EPA authorised the Army to move forward with the explosions, originally scheduled for November 20.
The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).
They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.
The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted a pause on Friday. But in a Saturday court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the Army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.
“The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay,” the Justice Department said in its filing.
But Earthjustice has argued that such a manoeuvre would sidestep the court’s authority.
Government lawyers have “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review”, lawyer Rachel Rintelmann wrote in a Friday filing.
A crisis ‘of the Army’s own making’
The controversy centres on a deteriorating stockpile of explosives stored for more than two decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.
The stockpile contains roughly 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of lead azide across 68 barrels, with lead accounting for approximately 6,900 pounds (about 3.1 tonnes) of its chemical mass.
The explosives had been kept in a mixture of water and ethanol to ensure their stability. But in March, military technicians at the facility discovered that the system was breaking down.
According to a court declaration, an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form.
That recrystallisation puts the lead azide at risk of exploding on its own, as a result of temperature charges or even friction. So many crystals had formed that it was no longer safe to even open the barrels, according to the expert.
But on Sunday, Earthjustice released a statement questioning how this problem was allowed to develop in the first place.
“This emergency is of the Army’s own making,” the statement said. “The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. ”
The US Army has said the barrels are set to be detonated in place at the Iowa facility.
But it claims to have explored other options as well. According to the Army’s environmental assessment, it has previously considered two alternatives: chemically neutralising the explosives, or transporting them to an on-site detonation facility.
It rejected both ideas due to concerns that handling or transporting the explosives could trigger an accidental detonation.
Burying the drums, meanwhile, risked subjecting the shock-sensitive material to jolts that could similarly cause an unintended explosion.
What should residents do before and after the explosions?
But the health risks of even a planned explosion have put residents and environmental groups on edge.
On November 15, the Army released two plume maps outlining the potential spread of lead contamination across a swath of eastern Iowa, though projections hinge on real-time wind conditions.
The first map traces what could happen if a lead-bearing plume drifts northward, with a potential airborne trajectory over communities like Burlington, Muscatine, Davenport, Iowa City and Cedar Rapids.
The second map presents a more tenacious problem: surface exposure.
As the plume tracks north, heavier lead-bearing particles are expected to coat the landscape, landing on outdoor furniture, cars, soil

items.text:
Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.
The death of Fiona, a beloved hippopotamus who captured hearts, has renewed calls to remind zoo visitors that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.
Fiona, 9 years old, died Thursday after ingesting a hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo. The zoo said that the hat was lodged in the hippo's small intestine and surgery was not possible.
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a statement.
While deaths are rare, items such as coins, shoes and sunglasses frequently fall, and sometimes are tossed, into animal enclosures.
In 2024, 70 U.S. coins were successfully removed from an alligator at Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium. And in 2025, a Komodo dragon ate a shoe that was thrown into its habitat at the Memphis Zoo. The shoe was removed and the dragon survived.
Dr. Gabriella Flacke, an associate veterinarian at Zoo Miami, said the zoo's staff have retrieved items such as cellphones from alligators.
"We've had to remove those items both endoscopically, which is basically putting a camera through the mouth and down into the stomach to grab and retrieve those items, or we've in a few cases had to do surgery where they were larger items that couldn't be removed that way," Flacke told NPR.
Recovering items from an alligator is easier than a hippo, she said. Unlike the alligator, which has a digestive system with one stomach divided into two parts, hippos have a multichambered stomach. This can make retrieving objects, such as the small hat that Fiona ingested, difficult, according to Dr. Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.
"It's not necessarily always the shape or size of the object, but it's maybe the twists and turns, metaphorically and physiologically, that things have to go through," Quammen told NPR.
Be aware that the animals have specialized dietary needs and requirements that caretakers provide them, Flacke said. She also asked visitors to follow zoo etiquette and not yell or throw objects at the animals.
"Anything that we bring that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful and not have your sunglasses on your head if you're leaning over and looking at something," she said. "If your child has a toy in its hand and you're walking around, it could just decide to throw the toy, whether it's thinking about that or not."
It's not just dangerous for zoo animals
Both Quammen and Flacke said people should not only be mindful of items that can harm animals at the zoo, but also what could hurt animals in the wild or pets at home.
Animals explore the world by putting things in their mouths, making them naturally curious about items that can be dangerous, Quammen said.
To help prevent an animal from ingesting something dangerous, one should dispose of their trash and properly store items such as human medicines in a place where an animal cannot reach it.
"Don't feed an animal without permission and that includes our pets at home, but also wildlife," added Quammen

Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the countr
items.text:
Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
Polish confirmation comes after Copenhagen reveals alleged Russian plot to kill US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil.
Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil.
The alleged assassination plan targeted Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and US citizenship, according to Danish media.
Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Maciej Wewior confirmed the alleged plot to kill Vasiliev in Poland to The Associated Press news agency on Sunday.
On Friday, in response to Denmark’s statement about the alleged assassination plan, Poland’s Foreign Ministry had written, “It is the second assassination attempt against the same person. The first one was foiled on the Polish territory in August 2026.”
It also said that a Russian national had been arrested.
Polish authorities detained the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.
Denmark announced the expulsion of a Russian diplomat on Friday after it accused Moscow intelligence of plotting the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September.
Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said on the same day that it suspected Russia of planning the assassination with the help of a banned Danish gang.
Two Danish men appeared in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder.
Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying they were unsubstantiated.
Previously, on August 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed that a plot to kill a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw was thwarted. He did not disclose Vasiliev’s name at the time but said the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government.
Support for Ukraine
Vasiliev has expressed his support for Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing war on the country and was performing across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.
Russia’s domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defence enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU.
Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations.
Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told reporters on Friday that Denmark was also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians.
Poland’s Foreign Ministry said it backed the move.
“Poland supports measures Denmark suggested to limit the access and freedom of travel of Russian nationals on the EU territory,” it said on X.
Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia has denied those accusations.

items.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
items.summary: When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threaten
items.text:
When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.
But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.
“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.
Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.
Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.
Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.
“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.
Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.
After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.
“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

items.summary:
WHO chief calls for peace amid heavy fighting in Ebola-hit DR Congo region
Fighting near DRC hospital disrupts Ebola efforts, putting patients and workers at ‘grave risk’, WHO warns.
The World Health Organization (WHO) chief has urged peace following heavy fighting in the Democratic Republic of the
items.text:
WHO chief calls for peace amid heavy fighting in Ebola-hit DR Congo region
Fighting near DRC hospital disrupts Ebola efforts, putting patients and workers at ‘grave risk’, WHO warns.
The World Health Organization (WHO) chief has urged peace following heavy fighting in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s (DRC) northeastern province, the epicentre of the Ebola outbreak.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Sunday that fighting near a hospital in the DRC’s Ituri province disrupted Ebola response efforts and forced health workers and aid partners to shelter inside a maternity ward for more than 24 hours.
“Heavy fighting has been ongoing since yesterday in the vicinity of a hospital in Ituri – in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged,” Tedros said on X.
“The situation has disrupted the work of the hospital and the wider Ebola response, putting patients, families and health workers at grave risk.”
Medical staff have been sheltering for their lives in a maternity ward in the facility for more than 24 hours, and the WHO is working to arrange a safe exit for the team and “for the hospital facilities, staff and patients to be protected,” Tedros also said.
“The best medicine is peace,” he added.
‘High-level transmission continues’
As of November 17, the WHO reported a total of 5,678 deaths out of 11,613 cases in the DRC, the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country.
The WHO said in a statement on Saturday that “while some areas had seen a slight decline in cases, sustained, high-level transmission continues overall in the country.”
Ituri and North Kivu, in the eastern part of the DRC, remain the most affected provinces.
The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread across swaths of the DRC’s east and northeast, which have been plagued by violence for more than 30 years.
Earlier in November, armed men thought to be linked to an ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated group raided villages and killed dozens of people in North Kivu, forcing patients with confirmed and suspected Ebola infections to flee.
The outbreak is also occurring amid ongoing fighting between government forces and the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group, which has seized key cities in eastern DRC, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult.

items.text:
South Korea’s stock market tumbles as AI bubble fears mount
The Kospi falls more than 3 percent as markets across the region brace for losses.
South Korea’s stock market has opened to sharp losses as markets across Asia brace for volatility amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI boom.
The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (Kospi) fell as much as 3.7 percent in early trading on Monday, continuing Friday’s tech-led sell-off across the Asia-Pacific region and in the United States.
The Kospi’s retreat came as investors anticipated volatile trading across the region upon the opening of key markets in Taiwan, China and Hong Kong later on Monday morning.
On Friday, the Kospi closed down 5.2 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 and Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled 5.1 percent and 6.2 percent, respectively.
On Wall Street, the benchmark S&P500 closed 3.7 percent lower for its seventh straight loss, while the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.3 percent to erase all of its gains for 2026.
Investors have long been concerned that tech firms may not be able to sustain the multi-trillion-dollar investments they have poured into infrastructure to power AI.
Concerns that the AI boom may be running out of stream have been exacerbated by expectations that the incoming Democratic-led US Congress will push for tighter regulation of the sector and the alleged spying scandal roiling chip giant Nvidia.
More to follow…

Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some lo
items.text:
San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
- Published
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.
But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.
Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
- Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting? 
  - Published4 days ago
- Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring 
  - Published9 July
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?
One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".
Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.
One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.
"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.
Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.
"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."
As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. Bu

Douala, Cameroon – Collins Mbah says he hunted down and killed several Cameroonian soldiers in the English-speaking Northwest region during his time as a separatist fig
items.text:
Cameroon’s ex-rebels caught between hiding and broken promises
Cameroon’s former rebels face arrest fears and failed reintegration.
Douala, Cameroon – Collins Mbah says he hunted down and killed several Cameroonian soldiers in the English-speaking Northwest region during his time as a separatist fighter between 2016 and 2020. Today, in the coastal city of Douala, the man in his mid-30s, who went by the name Commander No Sorrow, has taken on a different role: traditional healer, tending to lives rather than taking them.
Mbah says he abandoned the armed struggle after realising that fellow fighters were turning against the very people they had set out to protect. But he has firmly ruled out joining the government’s disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) programme.
“Quitting the struggle and joining the government disarmament programme would have meant I betrayed the people,” said Mbah, who dropped out of secondary school to join the revolt. “I don’t want to have anything to do with the government or the struggle any more. All I need now is peace of mind,” he told Al Jazeera.
October marked a decade since protests erupted in Cameroon’s English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions, eventually escalating into an armed conflict between separatist fighters and government forces.
The unrest began in late 2016 after Anglophone lawyers and teachers protested against the appointment of Francophone magistrates unfamiliar with British common law to courts in English-speaking regions, and French-speaking teachers unable to communicate fluently in English to schools there. The protests were met with a government crackdown and eventually gave rise to a separatist movement seeking independence for the two regions, which its supporters call “Ambazonia”.
The conflict has killed thousands of people, displaced hundreds of thousands and disrupted education across the two English-speaking regions, according to humanitarian and human rights organisations. New figures released in October by the Cameroonian nonprofit Centre for Human Rights and Democracy in Africa (CHRDA) suggest the death toll could be as high as 10,000.
The fighting remains deadlocked, with separatist groups continuing attacks and kidnappings while the government pursues a military campaign. Alongside its military operations, the government has launched a community dialogue initiative, after distancing itself from Swiss- and Canadian-supported peace efforts.
Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute launched the initiative in Buea, the capital of Southwest, in September and in Bamenda, the capital of the Northwest, on October 15. Local leaders are being encouraged to persuade fighters to surrender and enter DDR centres. At the two events, 55 fighters – 25 in the Southwest and 30 in the Northwest – were presented as having renounced the armed struggle.
Life beyond the battlefield
Despite leaving the rebellion, Mbah says he remains on the government’s wanted list. Without a national identity card, the father of three struggles to move freely around Douala and occasionally ventures into the outskirts to collect traditional herbs.
“I was initiated into traditional healing during childhood. The amulets and concoctions helped me foresee any danger when I was on the war front. Today, I use the same to heal,” he said. “But I don’t stay in a particular neighbourhood for long – I always move to the next to avoid being caught.”
Mbah is among former fighters who have chosen to reintegrate into society independently rather than enter government-run rehabilitation centres. Many say they fear arrest or poor treatment if they surrender.
Peter Mosongo, 28, now works as a motorcycle taxi rider in Buea after leaving the struggle in 2019. He joined in 2018 to protect his family but quit after witnessing what he describes as the indiscriminate killing of civilians by fellow fighters.
“I received threats from the fighters when I quit. They even kidnapped my father to force him to produce me,” Mosongo said. “I didn’t join DDR upon quitting out of fear that I may end up in prison. It was also being rumoured that those who surrendered were being killed silently.”
Mosongo says he also lost two cousins to the conflict.
Another former fighter, Richard Bende, left in 2019 because he believed the rebellion had become a “scores-settling venture”. He had fought government soldiers in Bamusso, in the Southwest, and now works as a secondary school history and geography teacher. Like Mbah and Mosongo, he avoided the DDR programme, citing concerns about the treatment of former fighters at its centres.
Broken promises inside DDR centres
Paul Mukete, who fought in Kumba from 2017 to 2020 under the nickname King of Vultures, chose a different path. But six years after entering the DDR programme in Tiko town, in the Southwest, he says he has little to show for it.
Apart from learning poultry and pig farming, Mukete says he has received no psychological care.
“We gave intelligence information to the military, who used it to kill some separatist fighters who refused to lay down their weapons,” he said. “We were about 600 in the DDR centre, but many have since left out of frustration. Some even rejoined the struggle and got killed.”
The 29-year-old father of three now takes on odd jobs to support his family.
His account raises questions about whether the programme is providing former fighters with the support they need to rebuild their lives and remain out of the conflict.
Fonbeh Hedwick Chia, a mental health specialist and founder of the Bamenda-based Living Vine Mental Health Services, says both fighters and civilians in the English-speaking regions have been exposed to psychological trauma.
He argues that the DDR centres lack the therapeutic support needed to rehabilitate former fighters, estimating that about 800 have renounced the armed struggle.
“The government is more concerned with the propaganda made when they come to the DDR than their integral welfare,” Chia told Al J

items.summary:
Trump criticises Schumer amid push for new Democrat leadership in US Senate
Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus since 2017, faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen in his bid to be the next Senate majority leader.
Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the United States Senate, is facing backlash
items.text:
Trump criticises Schumer amid push for new Democrat leadership in US Senate
Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus since 2017, faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen in his bid to be the next Senate majority leader.
Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the United States Senate, is facing backlash against his bid to serve as Senate majority leader in the incoming Congress.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump added to the ongoing criticism of Schumer’s leadership, signalling there would be tension with the White House if Schumer were picked again to lead the Democratic caucus.
“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”
The debate over Schumer’s leadership has underscored divides within the Democratic Party, particularly in the wake of the November 3 midterm elections.
Following a historic set of victories, Democrats are set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
Schumer, who leads the Democratic Senate minority, is hoping to retain his leadership position. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for December 1 to decide the majority leader.
A senator representing New York since 1999, Schumer has expressed confidence in his odds, saying he has the necessary votes to stay in charge.
“I will be elected majority leader,” Schumer told reporters last week.
But critics say Schumer, who will turn 76 on Monday, is ill-suited to lead a Senate Democratic caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, backed by progressives, has mounted a campaign to challenge Schumer for the majority leader role.
Van Hollen told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that he, too, was confident of winning.
“If you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change. They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate,” he said.
Schumer has also seen falling public approval ratings. In mid-November, a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos found that 34 percent of self-identified Democrats viewed Schumer favourably. That percentage was down from 38 percent in February.
November’s poll also suggested that 43 percent of Democrats held an unfavourable view of Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017.
The Senate Democratic leader is the only unresolved role among Congress’s top four positions.
House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress.
Meanwhile, John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans, and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

items.text:
A 'wow' player - why Ngumoha is already a Liverpool game-changer
- Published
Rio Ngumoha is going to be a 'wow' player for Liverpool - and he showed everyone exactly what he is already capable of in Sunday's 4-0 win over Manchester United.
He made an outstanding assist then added a fine finish, and there is much more to come. He plays without fear so he is going to score and make many more goals the same way.
Ngumoha has only just turned 18 but he is already a game-changer, someone who gets people excited because he is so hard to stop when he is one-on-one.
Of course he can frustrate you at times too, but that's what creative and explosive wingers like him do - and it's because he is so talented that everyone wants to see an end product from him every time he gets on the ball.
There were times against United when Ngumoha did not quite deliver, but he is still so young and I would much rather see players like him take too many touches - or try too many things and fail - than be afraid to try them in the first place.
So, if he runs out of play or runs into too many players at times, because teams are doubling up on him like United were, that just shows how scared they are of him.
His ability means he occupies opposition players - Youri Tielemans was always backing up Diogo Dalot on his wing to try to help him out, but that just meant United were leaving someone else free.
Sometimes it is actually harder when you are playing out wide against 10 men because you don't get the same amount of space - United were not attacking the same way they would have done with 11, and they were sitting in more.
Yes, Ngumoha ran up the odd blind alley or got outnumbered but that is always going to happen. As he learns, and gets even better, his decision-making will improve too. He will know when to try to go past people or when to find that free man instead.
But he still showed all the bravery you want from a winger against United and, when you keep trying things the way he did, something is going to come off for you.
I look at Bradley Barcola in a similar way to Ngumoha - he can be frustrating but he tries things, and can be brilliant.
For Liverpool right now, one of the biggest positives is the competition they have in wide areas, with those two plus Victor Munoz and Cody Gakpo.
There are other areas of their squad, like left-back or central midfield, where that competition needs to improve, but I don't really worry about the wide attacking areas in the same way.
Sunday was only Ngumoha's second Premier League start of the season, and his first since the opening day.
He maybe only got his chance because Gakpo has a calf problem but, when everyone is fit, it is really exciting that they will all be thinking they have to play their best to push the manager and get in the team.
'An important day for a positive mindset'
There were plenty of other positives for Liverpool, too. All in all, Sunday could not have gone much better for them.
United made a woeful start with poor concentration and mistakes which cost them but, from there, Liverpool saw the game out well.
Just because the opposition has a man sent off early on does not mean any kind of victory is a given, let alone a 4-0 win.
Look at how United's 11 men lost to City's 10 in the Manchester derby earlier this season - we've seen many times how good teams can frustrate a side with an extra player like that.
It definitely does not mean you are going to steamroller them, but Liverpool did that and made an abundance of chances to get even more goals.
Days like this are so important for building belief in all their attacking players, especially because they were playing at home, and against their big rivals.
Up until now, it had felt like Liverpool's better days this season had come on the road, but now the pressure and expectation is off them a bit - particularly if, like Ngumoha or Florian Wirtz, you have scored and played well.
I know from experience that, the next time they go back to Anfield, they will be buzzing. You know that the fans are already with you after you've scored against United, and you feel the love a little bit more.
This is the start of a big week for Liverpool and Iraola will probably make changes against Club Brugge in Belgium on Wednesday, knowing how difficult Sunday's Merseyside derby will be.
Everton is always a tough game but I think Liverpool will enjoy their trip to Hill Dickinson Stadium, and the confidence they will have after beating United will mean they can go there with a really positive mindset.
Danny Murphy was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
- Published
The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.
The deal is a "choice between
items.text:
Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
- Published
The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.
The deal is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.
He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.
The PM described it on Friday as a "win-win" deal with the EU on British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. But since then a host of politicians have criticised the plan, with one former prime minister urging him to "move on" from Brexit.
Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".
"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.
He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".
He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
But his announcement on Friday was greeted with a chorus of criticism from a number of opposing political figures.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was unfair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels.
She questioned the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
Badenoch accused him of having "plucked that figure out of the air" before saying "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Meanwhile Reform UK leader Farage called the deal a "very good day for the EU", before adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added in a social media post: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Over the weekend former prime ministers including Theresa May, Sir Tony Blair and Rishi Sunak also criticised the EU-UK deal.
May, who presided over three years of Brexit negotiations during her premiership, said she was "aghast" by the deal and warned Andy Burnham should "move on".
Sir Tony, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told The Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.
Badenoch will use her speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.
She will accuse the prime minister of securing a "terrible" deal and will say he should be "aiming a lot higher" in terms of driving growth.
Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses.
Rejoining the EU will hit the small firms that do not even trade with Europe with more red tape, more compliance costs, more Brussels rules they never asked for, he is expected to say.
On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.
He was also clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".
He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

items.text:
Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN:
We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
Microsoft and the US government agree there are more outages to come.
“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages to CBS, but sounded a much more ominous tone.
“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”
While the outages over the last week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.
The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets.
Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.

items.summary:
Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin
Sunday’s dinner is the third private event for top holders of the $Trump meme coin, launched shortly before his second inauguration.
United States President Donald Trump will host a third private dinner for top investors in his meme co
items.text:
Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin
Sunday’s dinner is the third private event for top holders of the $Trump meme coin, launched shortly before his second inauguration.
United States President Donald Trump will host a third private dinner for top investors in his meme coin $TRUMP, reigniting questions about potential conflicts of interest with his cryptocurrency ventures.
Sunday’s gala will take place at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, DC.
According to the dinner’s official website, the top 185 meme-coin holders will be invited to a gala dinner, where guests will include businessman Kevin O’Leary and boxer Floyd Mayweather.
The top 29 holders, meanwhile, will be given special access to a VIP reception where Trump will reportedly be present.
“There will be no private meetings with The President. No gifts will be accepted,” the website said of the VIP reception.
The event has been billed as “a once-in-a-lifetime experience — an evening you will talk about forever”.
But Democrats have accused the Republican leader of leveraging his public office for profit in violation of federal law. They see such dinners as an opportunity for private interests to pay for access to the president.
“Trump is continuing to exploit the presidency for his personal gain,” Kendall Witmer, the deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said in a statement.
In October, shortly after the gala was announced, eight Democratic senators issued an open letter promising to investigate any conflicts of interest such an event might raise.
“President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering,” the letter said.
The Democratic Party has since won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm race, paving the way for possible inquiries and subpoenas when the new members are sworn in next year.
Trump’s White House has dismissed the criticism, calling the dinner a “private event, not a government function”. It has also emphasised that “there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending”.
Trump has also argued that many of his assets are held in a trust while he is in office, though that trust is largely run by his family members.
The president is a stakeholder in cryptocurrency firms like World Liberty Financial, and has made promoting cryptocurrency a central part of his second term.
Under his leadership, the US Treasury established a reserve of digital currency assets, as part of Trump’s effort to make the US the “crypto capital of the world”.
Sunday’s gala is believed to be the third such dinner for top $Trump meme coin holders.
Meme coins trade on a popular likeness from the internet. Trump launched his on January 17, 2025, days before the start of his second term.
To encourage meme-coin purchases, Trump and his business partners held private events on May 22, 2025, and again on April 25, 2026, for top holders of the cryptocurrency.
The first was held at the same Trump golf club outside Washington, DC, and the second took place at Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida resort.
The May 2025 dinner reportedly required a minimum of $55,000 in $Trump coins to attend.
At the time, Chinese crypto investor Justin Sun was declared the winner of a “contest” for who held the most $TRUMP coins. Sun held about $18m of the coin in 2025, as well as tokens from World Liberty Financial.
Earlier this year, Sun sued World Liberty Financial, saying it had frozen his access to the assets he owned with it, making it impossible for him to sell them.
Trump’s inauguration in January 2025 proved a major boost for his coin, pushing its value to $74.
The $Trump coin has since lost value. On the eve of the gala dinner, it is worth about $0.88.
According to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year, Trump earned more than $2.2bn in 2025, the first year of his second term.
Much of that wealth came from meme coins, tokens and other digital assets. Some $636m came from $Trump meme coin sales.

items.text:
Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 with North Carolina seat
At least 258 US House seats are now under Democratic control, with four more midterm races yet to be decided.
The Democratic Party has won at least 258 seats in the United States House of Representatives, its highest total since 1992.
On Sunday, a congressional race in North Carolina was decided after a recount, giving Democrats their 258th House seat, as a handful of races in the 2026 midterm elections are still being counted.
The race for North Carolina’s 5th congressional district saw Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeat Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx, who has served 11 terms in Congress.
The win was symbolic of a larger political shift in North Carolina and elsewhere, as longtime Republican strongholds flipped to Democratic hands, sometimes for the first time in decades.
Foxx was first elected in 2004, and in recent years, she was the chair of the House Rules Committee. According to The Associated Press news agency, only 330 votes separated Hubbard and Foxx as of Sunday, when the race was called in the Democrat’s favour.
Four House races have yet to be called, meaning Democrats may still expand their already sizeable majority in the 435-member House.
The party has now picked up about 47 House seats. Currently, in the outgoing Congress, Democrats hold 214 seats.
But the House was not the only congressional chamber to flip in this year’s midterm elections.
In the 120th Congress, set to be sworn in on January 3, Democrats will also hold 56 seats in the US Senate, its largest majority in more than a decade.
Those majorities give the Democratic Party significant power over legislation, although President Donald Trump, a Republican, has already pledged to veto bills the party puts forward.
Experts say the Republican Party’s drubbing in the midterm elections was driven by voter frustration with issues like the cost of living, the US-Israel war on Iran, corruption and immigration raids.
It was also widely interpreted as a referendum on Trump’s second term, which began in 2025.
As of November, only 32 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance, according to a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos.
Democrats have framed their electoral victory as a unique opportunity to shape the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive who won her re-election bid in New York’s 14th congressional district, called the political shift a “mandate for change”.
“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the US Capitol.
The party’s majority in the House will be larger than any since Democrat Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 with a 258-seat majority for his party.
It is also just above the 257 seats held by Democrats when Barack Obama was elected in 2008.

Rasmus Hojgaard holds a share of the lead heading into a weather-delayed final day of the RSM Classic, with England's Marco Penge in contention as he looks to secure his PGA Tour future.
Hojgaard entered the week 122nd in the FedExCup standings and among the players looking to break into the top 100 and remain fully exempt on the PGA Tour next season, with the Dane now in prime position to do that.
The Ryder Cup star posted a five-under 65 on the Seaside Course at Sea Island Golf Club, firing five birdies to move to 13 under alongside Michael Thorbjornsen, with Max Greyserman a shot off the pace in third.

"Today felt very free - tomorrow's a completely different day," Hojgaard said. "I'm going to feel the nerves. I think that's what we all play for is to put ourselves in those positions, and we'll see what happens."

Fifa to confirm UK as host for 2035 Women's World Cup
- Published
Fifa is set to confirm on Monday that a first football World Cup will be hosted in the United Kingdom since 1966.
England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are the only bidders to jointly stage the 2035 Women's World Cup.
A delegation will be present at Fifa's Zurich headquarters with national associations holding a specially arranged virtual meeting, and voting to ratify the co-hosts.
The tournament would involve 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.
Nineteen venues are proposed by the 'All Together' bid, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.
Fifa's evaluation of the bid, published earlier this month, rated it 4.3 out of five. However, its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed that "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".
This is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.
Fifa's bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.
"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.
"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."
England hosted the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.
England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland are also joint hosts of the men's European Championship in 2028.
Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.
"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."
The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.
If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it will still be considered in its current form.
A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.
Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium the two Welsh venues.
Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "Wales has been a football nation for 150 years and we have never hosted anything on this scale. World Cup football played here, in front of Welsh children, would change what this game looks like in Wales: in the clubs, in the schools, and in the number of girls who grow up seeing a pathway into it."
Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time for the tournament - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.
The Irish Football Association's chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country. Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that."
Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow are the Scottish venues proposed, with Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell saying hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".
He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."
The special meeting of Fifa's Congress is also set to approve the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

items.title: Price looking to continue trend of Grand Slam victors tasting Worlds glory
items.summary:
Gerwyn Price looking to continue trend of Grand Slam victors tasting World Darts Championship glory
Gerwyn Price won the Grand Slam of Darts with a 16-11 victory over Gian van Veen; the last four winners of the Grand Slam have gone on to win the World Darts Championship at Alexandra Palace; Price is
items.text:
Gerwyn Price looking to continue trend of Grand Slam victors tasting World Darts Championship glory
Gerwyn Price won the Grand Slam of Darts with a 16-11 victory over Gian van Veen; the last four winners of the Grand Slam have gone on to win the World Darts Championship at Alexandra Palace; Price is hoping to continue the trend
Sunday 22 November 2026 22:10, UK
An interesting trend has occurred over the last four years: The winner of the Grand Slam has gone on to win the World Darts Championship.
It started with Michael Smith back in 2022, with Luke Humphries continuing it in 2023.
Of course, Luke Littler's back-to-back triumphs in Wolverhampton in 2024 and 2025 were then followed by him lifting the Sid Waddell Trophy.
- Gerwyn Price roars to fourth Grand Slam of Darts title
- Grand Slam of Darts Final 2026 - As it happened!
- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results
- Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW
Gerwyn Price wants to continue that in 2026.
Price roared to a 16-11 victory over Gian van Veen in the final of the Grand Slam, hitting five massive ton-plus checkouts in a confident display.
The win moves Price up to world No 3 ahead of Humphries and marks his first major title in four years.
Alexandra Palace was immediately on Price's mind following his victory and he hopes to extend the trend into a fifth year and become a two-time world champion.
"The sweet thing about this is the last couple of years, whoever won has gone on to win the World [Championship], so....," Price said after beating Van Veen.
"If that happens, then I'll take six months out!"
"I am superstitious and I believe in stuff like that," he later added.
"I hope I am not the one to break the trend."
Price has been in some form in 2026, the Grand Slam marking his fourth major final of the year but his first victory.
The Welshman has maintained he is the most consistent player across 2026 and puts part of that down to the love he now gets from the crowd.
It is a very different story from when he last won a Grand Slam title five years ago.
"How different it is, the crowd right behind me and cheering me all the way. How things can change." Price added.
"I thought these days would happen, I just didn't know when. I am glad it happened sooner rather than later.
"It definitely helps and spurs you on to come out to a crowd who is right behind you rather than against you.
"I have had that for the last two-and-a-half years and hopefully it continues.
"People have just realised I am who I am, I wear my heart on my sleeve, and I don't do things to put people off which people think I did.
"I am the most consistent. I am not saying I am the best player.
"I am full of confidence, I am in some great form. I am the most consistent across this season."
'I have now got the media off my back, not the monkey'
With the form 'The Iceman' has been in, it is remarkable it had been so long since Price had last tasted major glory back in 2022.
While he says it did not bother him, being reminded by the "media" spurred him on.
Now, the narrative changes.
"You guys [the media] were putting pressure on me and reminding me I hadn't won a tournament in a long time," Price said.
"You probably spurred me on as well so thanks.
"I keep saying I am not bothered when I lose and I stand by that.
"Obviously it hurts to lose. I have now got you off my back, not the monkey."
