items.text:
Virginia reports first measles-linked death of 2026 in child younger than 5
The death comes within days of health experts stripping the US of its measles elimination status, amid an uptick in cases.
US loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setback
A young child has died in Virginia, marking the first case of a measles-related death in the southern state for the year 2026.
The Virginia Department of Health made the announcement on Friday, just days after the United States lost its designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.
State authorities declined to provide details about the child’s death, citing the family’s privacy. It was disclosed, however, that the child was younger than five.
Virginia has reported 220 cases overall this year, most of them in the central part of the state. The vast majority of the cases were among people not vaccinated against the virus.
They include 40 children ranging from infants to age four, and another 75 children aged five to 12, according to state health department data as of November 19.
“Virginia has not had a measles-related death since 1978,” according to Frederic Bertley, an immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry, a research centre in Ohio.
He added that the spread of measles is evidence that the virus is gaining a foothold and becoming a growing problem for the US.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported its eighth measles-related death of the year last week and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of November 20.
Wisconsin also reported two deaths in 2026, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death of 2026 in early November.
In that case, the victim was reportedly a seven-month-old child. It was the state’s first measles-related death in more than three decades.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.
It has also tracked more than 5,800 cases nationally in 2026, the most of any year since 1991.
In August, President Donald Trump issued an executive order reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccinations, falsely suggesting that the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine could be dangerous.
“You have the MMR; we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together, there could be a possibility they are quite lethal,” Trump said.
The CDC has said it remains committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said.
The CDC has provided approximately $100m in additional funding to state and local health departments since August to strengthen vaccination efforts, surveillance and outbreak response.

items.title: The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

items.text:
The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?
- Published
Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.
It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two goals in quick succession.
Should it have been a red card though?
Was there a case for the video assistant referee (VAR) to suggest it should be downgraded to a yellow?
Let's take a look at the incident, and what a referee takes into account before showing a red for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.
What happened and what will the officials have taken into consideration?
1 of 5
Ronald Araujo played a long ball upfield for Alexander Isak to run on to.
Isak took a touch, before Yoro bundled into the back of the Sweden international and brought him down.
Referee Sam Barrott did not hesitate, giving the foul and sending off Yoro.
Was there doubt that Isak would have taken control of the ball? If so, it should only be a caution.
There are four key considerations for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity:
- distance between the offence and the goal
- general direction of play
- likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball
- location and number of defenders and attackers
As Isak was running directly towards goal in a central position, and there was no covering defender, three of the factors were satisfied.
The question is about the "likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball".
The Liverpool striker took a heavy touch, which moved the ball a few yards ahead of him.
The touch came before contact from Yoro, so there is no case that the challenge caused Isak to over-run the ball.
The referee and the VAR, John Brooks, must therefore assess whether Isak would definitely have got to the ball ahead of Senne Lammens. And that if he had, it would have been a good scoring chance.
If there is any doubt, then it should not be a red card.
It is a borderline case, and as such the VAR would not be expected to intervene for a clear and obvious error.
Likewise, if the referee had shown a yellow the VAR would not get involved.
Former Liverpool and England midfielder Danny Murphy, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said there was "no doubt" about the red card.
Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville also agreed with the decision.
"Leny Yoro has to cover and he doesn't," Neville said on Sky Sports. "He reacts late and his anticipation is poor.
"It's so clumsy from Yoro. It's naivety, he just needs to get off the pitch. You're not going to get that turned around, no chance."
Have there been any similar incidents?
There have been a couple of very similar cases this season.
Brighton's Pascal Struijk was sent off at Sunderland through a VAR review after he brought down Wilson Isidor.
The Seagulls successfully appealed against that red card on the grounds that there was clear doubt that Isidor would have taken control of the ball before it ran through to goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.
Sounds quite similar.
Could Manchester United appeal against Yoro's red card? There's nothing to lose by doing so.
Despite the Football Association regulatory commission unanimously ruling the Struijk red card was wrong, the Premier League's key match incidents panel voted the VAR intervention was a correct call on a split 3-2 vote.
Ipswich's Issa Diop avoided a VAR red card for a foul on James McAtee against Nottingham Forest, when the referee disagreed with the video official, and believed there was a covering defender. Forest boss Oliver Glasner was adamant it had been a clear goalscoring opportunity.
It was the same referee, Thomas Bramall, for both of those incidents.
That shows just how subjective such decisions can be. It is often rare to get a real consensus.
Yoro can count himself a little unfortunate to get the red card.

items.title: Le Pen denies receiving leaked information from French interior ministry official
items.summary:
Le Pen denies receiving leaked information from French interior ministry official
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen on Sunday said she did not receive, nor ask for, confidential information on an investigation into her party from a senior interior ministry official. She however could not say if
items.text:
Le Pen denies receiving leaked information from French interior ministry official
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen on Sunday said she did not receive, nor ask for, confidential information on an investigation into her party from a senior interior ministry official. She however could not say if other party members had benefited from the leaks. Hugues Moutouh, the civil servant under suspicion, has denied the allegations and asked to be relieved of his duties pending a probe.
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen Sunday denied receiving confidential information from a civil servant suspected of leaking details of investigations to her National Rally (RN) party, while acknowledging she could not say whether others in the party had benefited.
"I have never received confidential information and I have never asked for confidential information," Le Pen told France 2 television and France Inter radio.
The civil servant under suspicion, Hugues Moutouh, is a former senior official at the interior ministry. He has been serving as prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region but on Saturday said he asked to be relieved of his duties.
Le Pen said on Sunday she did not know Moutouh personally, and in response to a questions about possible beneficiaries of leaked information in the RN and her inner circle she said: "I am unable to tell you that, since the investigation is ongoing."
The investigation was opened after a search in another case uncovered an email from a civil servant working under Moutouh at the ministry at the home of far-right figure Frederic Chatillon, who is close to the RN and its leader, a source close to the case told AFP Sunday.
In the email addressed to her superiors, the civil servant described her questioning by anti-corruption authorities in an investigation into suspected illegal funding of the RN's election campaigns, the source said.
Only three people, including Moutouh, had access to this email, information first reported by Le Monde and confirmed by the source.
The allegations come five months ahead of a pivotal presidential election, with Le Pen the frontrunner according to opinion polls.
Le Pen was convicted of corruption last year over a fake jobs scam at the European Parliament, but an appeals court shortened her ban on holding public office, enabling her to run.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

He and his wife, Soumaya
items.text:
Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.
He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.
Now there are four.
A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.
Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.
The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.
"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."
He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel.
"He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says.
Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years.
Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies.
It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.
A test case
The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over.
The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone.
When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.
Wrecked home
Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers.
Almost everything in the house had been destroyed. Appliances — the fridge, freezer and washing machine — had bullet holes in them. Some, along with furniture, had been pushed over the second floor balcony, smashing on the ground below.
Kadouh says they knew from satellite photos there was destruction in their village "but the level of destruction — we were not expecting that. Everything that could be broken they broke."
In the kitchen were shattered floor tiles and kitchen cupboards wrenched from the walls.
The fire appeared to be set as the soldiers were leaving. Blackened, burned food packets — fruit boxes and cans of energy drinks with Hebrew writing — were on the floor along with rotting sandwiches.
In their 18-month-old grandson's bedroom, soot from a scorched ceiling dripped down on walls decorated with images of hot-air balloons and teddy bears climbing ladders to the moon.
Yaghi shows a bullet — one of many she says she found throughout the house. The spent engine casing of a missile or a drone with English markings reading "propulsion unit – tactical" was found in one of the rooms.
There is no running water or electricity — Kadouh says the Israeli military destroyed the solar panels.
The Lebanese army told them that when it reentered the village many of the houses had been rigged to be blown up. It said it dismantled explosives left by Israeli forces in their house and others.
The Israeli army did not reply to NPR queries about why the house was damaged or set on fire. It said military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives.
Unable to enter the village while Israeli forces were there, Kadouh said he saw a tank in their courtyard from drone images posted on social media.
Even the trees destroyed
Yaghi says the Israeli army used a bulldozer to uproot the trees — including the pine trees which yield one of their most prized cash crops: pine nuts. When they had killed the trees, she says they demolished the family's garage and destroyed their tractor.
"We are back to square one," Kadouh says. "Starting from scratch."
Even more precarious, though, than when they started decades ago. Despite a ceasefire, smoke rises from a nearby village where Israel is still attacking.
Amid all the damage, the destruction of the family's trees cuts the deepest.
"I tended to them as if they were small children — they were all dear to me," Kadouh says.
Yaghi points out where there were fruit-bearing cactus, olive trees, a fig tree one of her sons brought from Italy, avocado trees and fields of thyme, avocado.
Up until a decade ago, almost everyone here grew tobacco, diversifying crops when that market collapsed.
"We raised our children through hard work and thank God all of them were educated," Yaghi says, noting with pride that they all became professionals.
She maintains a visceral connection to the land.
"Record this," she asks, walking next to rose bushes that have begun to bloom again. "Our land is a paradise with everything in it. Our life is this land. Our life

Luke Littler says "titles and legacy" are more important to him than money after joining forces with a youth unemployment charity to help those in his native north west of England.
Two-time world champion Littler, 19, and The Kings Trust have established the 'Luke Littler Opportunity Fund', which aims to assist young people in finding employment through practical job skills and work experience.
The world No 1, who will look for a hat-trick of titles at Alexandra Palace live on Sky Sports from December 11, told the Big Issue after becoming its youngest guest editor: "I just love what I do. Once that love for the game goes, then I'll obviously stop, whenever that is.

"It's just the drive, the momentum you get when I'm going on stage, knowing that if I hit this double, you're into the final or I'm world champion.

JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.
That nickname stems from A
items.text:
Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.
That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.
But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.
It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex. The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.
South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.
The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.
Now, not only are the children getting to practice their reading, some of them have tried their hand at writing their own stories.
The newly published authors sit up front, ready to sign the pile of freshly-printed books for sale and answer questions about their process.
Thirteen-year-old Fiona Mogane, the bespectacled author of "Lindani's Modelling Journey," is one of them.
"It's about a girl who discovered a lot of challenges throughout her journey," Fiona explains. One of those challenges is that the main character Lindani's mother is an alcoholic, spending what little money the family has on drink — including government grant money meant for her daughter's welfare. She also shouts at her daughter a lot, and sometimes Lindani worries she will follow in her mother's footsteps.
Fiona writes: "Sometimes a thought intrudes on Lindani's mind, telling her that if she took some alcohol, it would make her feel better and stand up for herself …. However Lindani always pulls herself out of that thought: she knows she is stronger than that."
Phelelisa Somana, one of the coordinators of the book project, says she was impressed with the maturity of Fiona's story.
"When I read her story it had a very deep theme that I didn't expect a child to delve into in a way that she did," says Somana.
It "definitely just reminded me just how much kids are a lot smarter than they think they are," she adds. "They notice a lot more than they think they do."
Learning "Ubuntu"
Fortunately, Fiona's tale has a happy ending. Dreaming of becoming the next Miss South Africa, her character Lindani decides to try and raise the money she needs to enter a modelling contest by baking scones and selling them to her neighbors.
"She believes deep down inside that each one of her homemade scones has something special that makes them really delicious," Fiona writes.
In the end, Lindani makes enough cash to enter the contest. She comes in second place and is crowned "princess."
"She is happy because she has proved to herself that she can make a way when it initially seemed there was none," Fiona writes.
In real life, Fiona — also keen on modeling — is being raised in Alex by a single mom. Alex has high crime rates and poor government services like water and electricity. The young teenager is all too familiar with the problems, but she says there are good things about township life too..
"Alex is a crowded place, but when you're in Alex, you can learn a lot of things," she explains. "You can learn how to have Ubuntu."
Ubuntu is an African philosophy centering on community well-being and shared responsibility. As Fiona puts it: "Ubuntu is to help other people when they are in need."
Fiona, whose favorite subject at school is English, says she'd like to go to university, maybe to study medicine. And there's another dream too.
"One day, if I grow up, I want to build a big house that will be having a room with its own books," she says.
Homes without books
Fiona didn't grow up with books at home. Two-thirds of South African children don't have books at home, according to one study by UNICEF.
They won't necessarily find them at school either.
Only about 15% of public schools in South Africa have a functioning library, according to government data.
The dire state of child literacy has its roots in the home. Many children have weak early learning foundations, according to the UNICEF study, and they have no exposure to books before starting primary school.
"When I became the minister of basic education in 2024 I was confronted by the statistic of 80% of 10-year-olds who cannot read for meaning in any language," Basic Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube told NPR.
The minister says the government is trying to tackle this problem by getting more kids into early learning programs.
"We're investing ten billion rand [$58 million] over the next three years on a massive haul out of early childhood development centers," Gwarube says.
Tebogo Selekane, an English teacher at Kwa-bhekilanga secondary school, says the weekend program at Read Alex has helped some of her students a lot. Two of her students have stories in the book.
"They are doing very well in reading," says Selekane. "There's a lot of change in them... they will respond back with confidence."

items.title: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
items.summary: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files wi
items.text:
The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.
Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
Creator Edmund McMillen claims he ‘had no idea’ AI music was used in the latest version of Binding of Isaac.
Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.
Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on S
items.text:
Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
- Published
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

items.title: ‘We don’t want personal kiosks’: Natembeya takes aim at DAP-Kenya, Ford-Kenya
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya has launched a fresh attack on Democratic Action Party of Kenya (DAP-K) leader Eugene Wamalwa, accusing him of running the party as a personal outfit rather than an institution serving the interests of Western Kenya and the country.
Nate
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya has launched a fresh attack on Democratic Action Party of Kenya (DAP-K) leader Eugene Wamalwa, accusing him of running the party as a personal outfit rather than an institution serving the interests of Western Kenya and the country.
Natembeya described DAP-Kenya and Ford-Kenya led by Speaker Moses Wetangula as personal kiosks, arguing that political parties in the region had been reduced to vehicles serving individual ambitions instead of providing a platform for collective political interests.
The governor said his differences with Wamalwa were rooted in disagreements over the direction and management of DAP-Kenya, revealing that he had sought a mandate to rebrand the party and strengthen its presence in the Western region.
“That opportunity was not there because it’s just a kiosk. DAP is just a kiosk, like Ford-Kenya is a kiosk. We don’t want kiosks that serve individuals in Western Kenya; we want political parties that serve the interests of the local people and the nation at large,” Natembeya said.
Speaking during an interview on Hot 96 , Natembeya claimed that DAP-Kenya had lost several senior officials, leaving Wamalwa as the only remaining figure at the top of the party’s leadership.
He said the party had experienced an exodus of officials, including deputy party leaders, the secretary-general, the organising secretary and the treasurer.
“Our current party, I think there’s only one person supposed to leave and lock the door the party leader because everybody else has left,” he said.
When asked to clarify whether he was referring to DAP-Kenya, Natembeya identified Wamalwa, whom he acknowledged was a principal in the opposition.
The governor also described himself as a principal in the United Opposition but said he had deliberately kept away from some of its engagements because he felt they had become dominated by competition over political positions.
“Even me, I’m a principal. I’m actually a principal in the United Opposition, I am. But I just refuse to sit there because it appeared as if we are jostling for something,” he said.
Natembeya said his fallout with Wamalwa was not personal but stemmed from differences over how DAP-Kenya should be managed and expanded.
He claimed he had played a significant role in mobilising opposition support against the Kenya Kwanza administration and wanted to use the momentum to build a stronger political platform in Western Kenya.
The governor said he had approached Wamalwa with a proposal that would allow him to take charge of rebranding and organising the party at the regional level while Wamalwa concentrated on national politics.
“Maybe I’ve done a bit of work there and people are accepting, can I be given the mandate to rebrand this party? You are going to be the candidate, go and play at the national level, let me play at the regional level in this party because in Kenya, politics is regional. Can I organize the Western region using this party because I need a platform?” he said.
Natembeya argued that the proposal should have been subjected to the party’s internal decision-making structures, allowing members to debate and determine the best way forward.
He said he had wanted the party to convene its National Executive Committee (NEC) and National Delegates Convention (NDC) to discuss the proposed changes and give members an opportunity to decide whether rebranding was necessary.
The governor, however, claimed that his proposal was frustrated by the party’s General Management Committee, which he accused of failing to provide a clear path for resolving the disagreements.
He said he was willing to accept an alternative proposal if party members believed DAP-Kenya could be strengthened without changing its leadership structure.
Natembeya also questioned the political influence of Ford-Kenya, arguing that its parliamentary representation had diminished its standing in national political negotiations.
He claimed that the party had only four Members of Parliament and described its role in the wider political landscape as insignificant.
“Actually, Ford-Kenya with four members of parliament, completely insignificant political players on the political chessboard. What was left there was DAP,” he said.
The governor further questioned Wamalwa’s claim to represent Western Kenya in opposition negotiations, arguing that political influence should be determined by the ability to mobilise and represent voters rather than previous government positions.
He criticised what he described as the practice of relying on past political offices, including parliamentary and ministerial positions, to claim influence in current political arrangements.
Natembeya also raised concerns about what he termed double standards in the opposition’s approach to ethnic politics, accusing some leaders of condemning tribalism while practising it.
“We are condemning tribalism and practicing it. We don’t want that,” he said.
He argued that Kenya needed to move away from a political culture in which voters supported candidates primarily because they came from their communities.
According to Natembeya, political leadership should be based on the ability of candidates to understand and address the needs of the entire country rather than their ethnic backgrounds.
“We want to change Kenya so that you don’t vote for an individual just because he comes from your community,” he said.
The governor said the country needed to build confidence in national leadership so that citizens could feel represented regardless of which community produced the President.
He argued that ethnic considerations had continued to shape electoral choices since independence, contributing to a political system in which community identity often takes precedence over accountability and governance.

items.text:
Russian vessel hit by suspected sea drone at Libya’s Benghazi naval base
There was no immediate reaction from Russia, and no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.
A suspected sea drone attack has hit a Russian vessel at a naval base in eastern Libya, causing an explosion and a brief fire, according to the North African country’s eastern-based government.
The Reuters news agency reported that an unidentified number of people were injured in the attack at the Benghazi naval base on the Mediterranean Sea on Sunday. The nationalities of the casualties were not immediately known.
The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya’s Benghazi-based administration, the eastern government said. It gave no details about the vessel or its cargo.
The administration said it had launched a joint investigation with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it”.
The government said the fire had been brought under control and the site secured, while it condemned the suspected strike as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety.
‘Exporting international conflicts’
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said, adding that Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used naval drones and missiles to target Russian warships and naval facilities in the Black Sea.
On Saturday, a drone struck a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland’s border guard attributed the strike to Ukraine.
A Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast in March after an attack that Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed on Ukraine, while last December, Ukraine said it had used aerial drones to strike a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.
Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011.
A United Nations-recognised government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

items.text:
'Rolls-Royce' Iqbal's 'dream' journey from Old Trafford to Tannadice
- Published
Given the superlatives being thrown in the direction of Zidane Iqbal by the Scottish football fraternity, one would think he was a replica of a certain France great instead of just sharing his name.
So much so that BBC Radio Scotland pundits were suggesting on Saturday's Sportsound that the 23-year-old is the answer to Celtic's hunt for a long-term successor to captain Callum McGregor as their midfield general.
It is just as well for Dundee United that the Iraq international is tied to them until at least the summer, his early season appearances for Utrecht ruling out a transfer during the January window.
So, where has he sprung from and what is all the fuss about?
- 'Goodwin due a lot of credit and kudos' 
  - Published3 hours ago
- Hibs 0-4 Dundee United: What Goodwin said 
  - Published1 day ago
Midfielder inspiring United 'masterclass'
Born in Manchester to a Pakistani father and an Iraqi mother, Iqbal came through the Old Trafford youth system.
He signed his first professional contract with United in 2021 and became the first British-born South Asian and first-ever British South Asian to play in the Champions League when he came on as an 89th-minute substitute against Young Boys that December.
However, that was to be his one and only first-team appearance and, although he had already made his international debut in a World Cup qualifier at the age of 19, he was sold to Utrecht for a reported fee of £1m in summer 2023.
Starting off in their Jong Utrecht second string, he would go on to make 49 appearances for the Dutch top-flight outfit before making a surprise switch to the Scottish Premiership this summer.
On the one hand, United were getting a player who played all three of Iraq's games at this summer's World Cup, two of them starts, albeit all three were heavy defeats.
On the other hand, Iqbal had only managed seven appearances last season for Utrecht and had been a second-half substitute in two of their four matches at the start of the new campaign.
However, after a pivotal display in what was being described as a midfield "masterclass" by United in Saturday's 4-0 dismantling of hosts Hibernian, manager Jim Goodwin revealed he always had belief the Tangerines were unearthing a "Rolls-Royce".
"The head of recruitment's job is to go and identify good talent for us," Goodwin told BBC Scotland. "It's my job to give him the profile and then he goes out and does the groundwork.
"We could see immediately when we watched the footage of Zidane and when we had the Zoom call with him and his representatives, we not only had a fantastic player but a really good person with the right characteristics to come and fit the culture here."
'Enjoy him while you can, United fans'
While on-loan Rangers man Lyall Cameron was among the goals and fellow 24-year-old Dylan Tait provided a stylish assist, it was the third leg of what some regard as the best midfield triumvirate in the Premiership who was singled out for most praise at Easter Road.
With former Celtic winger Aidan McGeady again pondering the question about McGregor's likely successor, transfer market expert and former United wing-back Allan Preston opined: "A six for Celtic? Look no further than young Iqbal.
"He's been magnificent since he's come to Scottish football, absolutely brilliant. Running the show again.
"If Celtic are looking for a young boy at his age with experience, he is a full international, knows the game, played in Scotland, you can see what he can do, there's your man in front of you.
"Other players' hair's on fire, but he's just nice and calm. He's at a different level. He doesn't panic. When the ball comes to him, he is so calm on it, he takes his time, he's got great peripheral vision."
The former Dundee United wing-back pointed out, though: "He's had his two clubs that he can play for in a year of football, so he is going nowhere until at least the summer, so enjoy him while you can because I think you'll get serious money for this young boy."
McGeady pointed to Iqbal's "good pedigree", having started with Manchester United and already having 32 caps for Iraq, but wondered if that would be enough for Celtic to consider him.
"I don't even think, if he's performing this well, Celtic will go and get him," said McGeady.
"Why are Celtic not looking at players like this? Do they feel they have to prove themselves somewhere else first?"
Former Celtic captain Scott Brown was similarly impressed.
"He's been a delight to watch - sharpness to get on the ball and willingness to drive forward," the former midfielder and manager pointed out.
"He beats a man in the middle of the park as well and there's not too many midfielders willing to do that.
"Watching him there talking to the media, he can't get the smile off his face. He enjoys football, he takes the ball under pressure, he does things that other people don't do, especially in midfield.
"He brings composure, but he can also drive through as well. His willingness to keep getting on the ball, even if he makes that slight mistake - that's what I really enjoy watching about him."
Drive from Netherlands to Scotland 'worth it'
While Goodwin reckons there will be likely interest in the summer, Iqbal has no thoughts of so quickly leaving a club - and manager - who have resurrected his club career.
"I'm not even looking at any other clubs," he told BBC Scotland. "I'm fully focused on Dundee United.
"They've given me a platform to enjoy myself and play football. I'm really enjoying my football again.
"They've given me faith and confidence. The gaffer and the coaching staff have a lot of belief in me.
"The bare minimum I can do is pay them back with strong performances and hopefully it carries on."
Iqbal recalled being at Manchester United's "development centre since I was four or five - I signed when I was eight", explaining that he "then left for some first-team football".

items.title: Blast on Russian ship in Benghazi a suspected drone attack, say Libyan authorities
items.summary:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya’s eastern-based government has said.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the suspected strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up the
items.text:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya’s eastern-based government has said.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the suspected strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
“Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred onboard a Russian ship docked in the port,” said the administration backed by the military commander Khalifa Haftar. “It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones.”
Authorities in divided Libya’s east said the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia, under maritime cooperation agreements between the two countries.
Two medical sources said no deaths had been reported from the blast, but there were injuries. The number and nationalities of those injured are not yet known.
There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.
The eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take legal and diplomatic measures against anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port.
A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.
Initial reports and footage suggest the ship was struck from above, potentially by a drone, launched no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port.
Russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean, which has a growing importance after it lost bases in Syria.
Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea continued to smoulder on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.
The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly injured.
On Sunday visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.
Pictures and video released earlier by the Finnish coastguard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannons during the night in an attempt to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
“Smoke is still coming from the vessel, and there is clearly still heat onboard,” said Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, a sea safety officer and commander of the maritime sub-centre Helsinki for the Finnish border guard, at a press conference on Sunday.
Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

Two goals inside seven minutes from Tajon Buchanan and Tani Oluwaseyi gave Villarreal a commanding lead at Camp Nou, and things got worse for Barça when winger
items.text:
Barcelona came back from two goals behind to beat Villarreal 3-2 at home on Sunday and restore their three-point lead at the top of La Liga.
Two goals inside seven minutes from Tajon Buchanan and Tani Oluwaseyi gave Villarreal a commanding lead at Camp Nou, and things got worse for Barça when winger Lamine Yamal missed a first-half penalty.
The Catalan giants fought back in style, striking three times in an 11-minute second-half spell to claim victory. Gerard Martín and Fermín López pulled Barça level before Pau Navarro’s own goal gave them victory.
Barca have now won four consecutive matches across all competitions since their Clàsico defeat by Real Madrid in October, and restored their three-point cushion over José Mourinho’s side, who had moved level with Saturday’s victory over Celta Vigo.
“We suffered because we started the game badly, we let in two goals very early. I’ll remember how the team reacted but we have to work to ensure this doesn’t happen again,” Barcelona midfielder Pedri told Dazn. “Against a team like this you can’t always turn things around from two down.”
Buchanan fired Villarreal ahead in the fifth minute, producing a perfect sliced effort from distance after López gave the ball away. Two minutes later, the visitors doubled their lead through another Canadian, as Oluwaseyi broke down the left flank and smashed an effort into the roof of the net.
Hansi Flick’s side should have pulled one back when Oluwaseyi felled Lamine Yamal in the area and a penalty was given after a VAR review. The teenager took it himself but dragged his spot-kick against the post and wide.
Barcelona came out invigorated for the second half and quickly dragged themselves back into the match. Pedri shot wide and Gulacsi saved López’s low effort before Martín headed home in the 57th minute from Pedri’s cross.
Four minutes later, López slammed home the second after being teed up by Lamine Yamal, and the third was quick to follow. Lamine Yamal’s clever backheel pass fed Eric García, whose cross was bundled into the back of his own net by Navarro, who was later sent off for a second yellow card to complete a miserable afternoon.
In Serie A, Juventus moved into the top six with a thumping 4-0 victory over Venezia as their recent upturn in form continued. Luciano Spalletti’s side were booed off after a goalless first half, but found four second-half strikes as their unbeaten run stretched to four games in all competitions.
Nick Woltemade sparked the game into life after coming off the bench, pouncing on a loose ball to smash home his second league goal in two games before turning provider for Teun Koopmeiners’ whipped finish. Juan Cabal headed home Juve’s third before Kolo Muani won and converted a penalty to complete the rout, with all four goals coming between the 53rd and 71st minute.
“In the first half, we gave the ball away too much,” Spalletti told Dazn. “It was crucial the players recognised something was missing … in the second half, the players were decisive and more relaxed.”
Milutin Osmajic scored twice in a 2-0 win for Genoa at Sassuolo, while Bologna were held to a 1-1 draw by Udinese, who climb off the bottom of the table at Venezia’s expense. Inter visit Atalanta and Milan host Frosinone in the evening kick-offs.
In Ligue 1, Paris FC climbed to second place behind local rivals PSG with a 4-0 home win over lowly Angers. Patrick Zabi, Luca Koleosho, Maxime Lopez and Diego Coppola all struck in the second half for Liam Rosenior’s high-flying side.
Musiala reportedly suffers further seizure
Bayern Munich’s Jamal Musiala reportedly suffered another seizure in training this week, according to information received by an AFP subsidiary on Sunday.
Musiala collapsed twice on the pitch in pre-season with the 23-year-old later revealing he had a “neurological disorder” which can lead to “temporary but treatable seizures”. Monday’s report incident was the second since he made the announcement; the player is reportedly adjusting his medication to properly treat the condition while continuing to play.
News of the incident comes as Bayern have faced criticism from footballers’ union Fifpro over what they claim is a “coordinated campaign” to pressure Musiala to renegotiate his 2025-extended contract.
On Friday, Bayern’s supervisory board member and former CEO, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge suggested the Germany interational may need to take a pay cut if he cannot recapture his old form.
“Based on what we know, it unfortunately suggests that it will be difficult for him to return to the level he so often demonstrated here in this stadium,” Rummenigge said. “If he doesn’t return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation … because frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable.” AFP
- This story will be updated

items.summary:
Libya: Suspected drone attack hits Russian warship in Benghazi
November 22, 2026
An explosion occurred early Sunday on a Russian ship at a naval base in Benghazi in eastern Libya due to a suspected drone attack.
"Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred on board a Russian ship doc
items.text:
Libya: Suspected drone attack hits Russian warship in Benghazi
November 22, 2026
An explosion occurred early Sunday on a Russian ship at a naval base in Benghazi in eastern Libya due to a suspected drone attack.
"Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred on board a Russian ship docked in the port," the eastern-based Libyan administration said in a statement.
"It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones."
According to medical sources, injuries were reported, but no deaths.
The statement added that, as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based Libyan government, the vessel had stopped at the Benghazi port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia.
Since the 2011 uprising that overthrew longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi, Libya has been divided between the UN-supported government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Local authorities condemn attack
The eastern-based administration said the port and naval base facilities in Benghazi, including the warehouses, were safe. They added that normal operations would resume once the fire was under control and the site was secured.
The authorities condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya's sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety. They said they would take legal and diplomatic measures against those responsible and would launch a joint investigation with Russia.
As of Sunday afternoon, no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.
The administration also stressed that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine or to any armed conflict beyond its borders. It said that its relations with friendly countries were a sovereign matter.
It said it would not allow "Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts."
Echoes of Russia's war in Ukraine
The incident in Benghazi occurred as Ukrainian forces increased their long-range attacks against Russia, extending far beyond the front lines.
On Saturday, a drone hit a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland's border guard said Ukraine carried out the attack.
In March, a Russian tanker was attacked in the Mediterranean near Maltese waters. Libyan officials at the time believed this to be a sea drone attack.

items.title: Genge eager for England to build on victory in All Blacks rematch
items.summary:
Ellis Genge calls on England to follow New Zealand victory with another win over All Blacks in Nations Championship
England thrashed New Zealand 37-12 at the Allianz Stadium on Saturday and will face each other again on Saturday, having both finished second in their respective Nations Championship g
items.text:
Ellis Genge calls on England to follow New Zealand victory with another win over All Blacks in Nations Championship
England thrashed New Zealand 37-12 at the Allianz Stadium on Saturday and will face each other again on Saturday, having both finished second in their respective Nations Championship groups; England also beat New Zealand last November
Sunday 22 November 2026 17:21, UK
Ellis Genge called on England to back up their record victory over New Zealand as they go in search of an unprecedented hat-trick against the All Blacks.
The rivals face an immediate rematch of England's 37-12 procession at Allianz Stadium that meant they each finished second in their Nations Championship pools, setting up the battle for third place on Saturday.
Following on from last November's 33-19 triumph, it was only the second time in the fixture's 121-year existence that England had registered consecutive wins - and Steve Borthwick's men are aiming to carve out their own piece of history.
- Nations Championship: Latest fixtures, results and schedule for final week
- Itoje warns against win-at-all-costs culture amid Sandpapergate saga
- Nations Championship: Schedule, results for rugby's inaugural tournament
"Try and emulate it, do the same thing again," Genge said. "It's as simple as it sounds. I don't think you can take anything away from New Zealand. They're not any less of a beast next weekend than what the challenge was this week.
"New Zealand tends to be one team that catches you off guard, but what shocks you is that they're actually quite direct.
"You think they're all traditionally very good at moving the ball, but they're very punchy and we got that right against them."
England delivered the best result of Borthwick's four years in charge by flattening the All Blacks to extend their winning run to five Tests and issue a warning that they will be genuine contenders at next year's World Cup.
But amid the euphoria that has greeted confirmation of their post-Six Nations revival, Genge will keep perspective - recalling the criticism their followed their 45-21 drubbing at Ellis Park in the Nations Championship opener.
"Sport's fickle in that sense," Genge said. "We were the worst team in the world against South Africa when we got hammered at their gaff about five months ago.
"Then we hammered Fiji because of a red card apparently, then scraped past Argentina and then now we're the best thing since sliced bread. It's one of them.
"Sometimes the outside noise can creep in. Sometimes it can build you up and that's a long way down to the bottom.
"You've got to try and just keep your head on your shoulders and just build results. We do as best as we can at the job to keep everyone's head on their shoulders, especially with a young squad.
"Some of us miserable old boys are a bit easier, but the boys get so excited to play and be a part of it, which is brilliant. You've got to prepare them for that as well."
Atkinson explains gladiator celebration
Seb Atkinson was the last of England's five tryscorers at Allianz Stadium and he marked the crowning moment of a stellar individual performance by sticking out his tongue and making a throat-slitting gesture.
The celebration has been mistaken online as a reference to the All Blacks' haka, but Atkinson revealed it was born out of his interest in gladiatorial combat and is deciding whether to make it his calling card.
"I've had a bit of stick already on that, so we'll see whether it stays," Atkinson said. "It's a gladiator celebration. I used to have a big interest in Roman history so it was bit of a gladiatorial theme from when they used to do it in the Colosseum.
"I enjoyed learning about that when I was growing up and I trialled it with Gloucester and then I felt like I had to give it a bit extra today [Saturday]."
Atkinson is expected to feature again for England against New Zealand next week and hopes the hosts can take a leaf out of South Africa's book by showing the hunger to evolve like the back-to-back world champions.
"Any professional team, any sporting team, always wants to strive to get better because a team that gets caught still is in trouble," he added. "That's what the South Africans have done really well over the last period.
"Their game has been transformed. We'll be focusing on ourselves, but with an eye just to keep getting better and see what we can do."

items.title: Drone strikes hit homes and UN building in Sudan's Khartoum
items.summary:
Drone strikes hit homes and UN building in Sudan's Khartoum
Drone strikes damaged residential homes and a United Nations building in Sudan's capital Khartoum early Sunday, with the army accusing neighbouring Ethiopia of launching the attacks. The strikes came as drone warfare intensifies in the coun
items.text:
Drone strikes hit homes and UN building in Sudan's Khartoum
Drone strikes damaged residential homes and a United Nations building in Sudan's capital Khartoum early Sunday, with the army accusing neighbouring Ethiopia of launching the attacks. The strikes came as drone warfare intensifies in the country's conflict, now in its fourth year.
Drones struck Sudan's capital Khartoum, damaging residential homes and a United Nations building on Sunday, witnesses and the world organisation said.
Explosions were heard in the area around Khartoum airport and other parts of the city from around 2:00 am until approximately 4:30 am.
A drone strike completely destroyed a house, a witness said, while a Sudanese army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.
"The drone attack at dawn today is a continuation of Ethiopian aggression against Sudanese territory, as the drones were launched from Ethiopia's Bahir Dar airport," the source told AFP.
Sudan's military has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), against which it has been fighting since April 2023, including through drone attacks launched from Ethiopian territory.
Ethiopia denies the accusations.
AFP footage showed a house reduced to rubble, with a security perimeter around the site. Pieces of furniture, household items and clothing were scattered among the debris.
Al-Nour Adam, who lives in the area, told AFP that upon entering the house after the strike, "we found a person lying on a bed, wounded in his left arm, chest and head".
Read moreUN refugee chief Barham Salih slams 'shameful' war in Sudan, urges 'political solution'
'Where are we supposed to go?'
"The strikes are indiscriminate," Adam said.
"A strike could hit while you are asleep. You might wake up to find your children gone... It is truly tragic. You cannot be certain of anything."
Yasser Hassan, another resident, said that the occupants of the house "had only just moved in, after searching for shelter for a long time".
"Then the drone struck them. Where are we supposed to go?"
Another witness reported that a drone hit the home of a mosque's muezzin, the person who calls Muslims to prayer, in Jebel Aulia, around 45 kilometres (28 miles) south of Khartoum.
"People were trying to rescue family members trapped under the rubble," the witness said.
The United Nations, meanwhile, said that "a UN premises with UN colleagues in the building was damaged".
"This occurred in a civilian neighbourhood," the UN's humanitarian office (OCHA) said in a statement posted on X.
OCHA condemned the risk posed to humanitarian workers, saying it was "unacceptable" that UN personnel were being exposed to such danger.
Saudi Arabia, which has provided support to the Sudanese regular army in the country's war, said on X that it "categorically rejects these brutal attacks".
Drone warfare
Authorities did not immediately report on casualties.
The conflict between the RSF and the Sudanese army has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.
The United Nations has repeatedly criticised both sides' rampant use of drones, which killed more than 1,100 people in the first half of 2026.
Of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes, the UN said.
Read moreEmirati diplomat could become next UN chief despite human rights concerns
A Sudanese army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village days ago, as the army pushed through the state, recapturing territory from the RSF.
The rival forces have for the last year wrestled for control of the resource-rich southern Kordofan region, which connects the army-held centre and east to RSF-controlled Darfur.
In recent months, both the army and the RSF have increasingly relied on drones capable of striking targets hundreds of kilometres away without risking their fighters.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.title: Gachagua: August polls should be a formality after DCP nominations
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has urged Mt Kenya voters to ensure the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) conducts competitive and credible nominations that produce strong candidates capable of winning elective seats, allowing them to focus on his presidential c
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has urged Mt Kenya voters to ensure the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) conducts competitive and credible nominations that produce strong candidates capable of winning elective seats, allowing them to focus on his presidential campaign ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Gachagua said he wants the party to attract several aspirants for every elective position to encourage competition and give voters an opportunity to choose candidates with the strongest support.
He said DCP intends to conduct free and fair nominations by the end of March 2027, insisting that the party’s electoral contest in the Mt Kenya region should effectively end at the nomination stage, with the August General Election serving as confirmation of the winners.
Speaking while addressing supporters, Gachagua challenged aspirants seeking various positions to prepare for competitive primaries, saying the party wants between five and eight candidates contesting for every ward.
“All our aspirants, we want every ward to have five, six, eight aspirants. We want a real contest! For MPs, sort it out and give me candidates!” he said.
The former Deputy President said the party’s objective was to produce candidates with strong electoral backing during nominations so they could immediately shift their attention to mobilising support for his presidential ambitions.
He argued that once candidates secure the DCP ticket, they should no longer worry about their individual races but instead concentrate on strengthening the party’s presidential campaign across the region.
“Nominations will be free and fair by the end of March, and our election here in the mountain will end at nominations. August is confirmation!” Gachagua said.
He outlined a mobilisation strategy that would require nominated candidates to campaign for his presidential bid, increase voter registration and turnout, and engage different groups within their communities.
According to Gachagua, aspirants who emerge victorious in the party primaries will be expected to help young people obtain national identity cards, address alcoholism and mobilise women to participate in the electoral process.
“I want all those people, once they are selected at nominations, to start campaigning for my presidential vote without worrying about their own seats,” he said.
“Once you give them the nomination, let them start working on my presidential campaign, securing voter turnout, fetching identity cards for the youth, curbing alcoholism and engaging electorate .”
The remarks signal Gachagua’s intention to use DCP’s nominations as an early mechanism for consolidating political support in Mt Kenya, with successful aspirants expected to become key organisers of his presidential campaign.
His strategy also places considerable importance on the party primaries, which could determine the strength of DCP’s candidates and its ability to mobilise voters across the region ahead of the August 2027 polls.
Gachagua has been seeking to consolidate his political influence in Mt Kenya following his fallout with President William Ruto, positioning DCP as a vehicle through which the region can negotiate its political future and challenge the current administration.

items.title: ‘Disappointing’: Delegates react after COP31 climate talks end without deal
items.summary:
‘Disappointing’: Delegates react after COP31 climate talks end without deal
Draft text considered too weak to deal with climate change after oil-producing countries oppose the term ‘fossil fuels’.
United Nations climate talks have failed to secure a deal on how to deal with climate change, prompting
items.text:
‘Disappointing’: Delegates react after COP31 climate talks end without deal
Draft text considered too weak to deal with climate change after oil-producing countries oppose the term ‘fossil fuels’.
United Nations climate talks have failed to secure a deal on how to deal with climate change, prompting UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to express “a very profound frustration”.
Multiple countries and negotiating blocs said on Sunday that the final draft, presented by COP31 presidents Turkiye and Australia, was too weak to fight global warming.
If the text had been approved, it would have acknowledged for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve from the 2015 Paris Agreement.
The talks had extended into overtime after key oil- and gas-producing countries opposed mentions of “fossil fuels” in the final text. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for funds to help poorer countries adapt to climate change.
The last time the annual UN climate talks failed to end in an agreement was in Copenhagen in 2009.
Here’s how countries and key parties reacted to the deal’s failure:
UN chief Guterres
“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” Guterres said.
The UN chief criticised powerful fossil fuel interests for obstructing climate action, accusing them of distorting scientific evidence, delaying policies and prioritising profits.
EU delegation
The European Union said it will not endorse a deal that “does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change, and we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel”.
A spokesman added that the draft deal “does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face”.
Denmark’s climate minister
Samira Nawa said the EU was willing to accept clauses on adaptation finance but argued that the text did not go far enough.
“This is about the mitigation. It’s about the fossil fuels not being mentioned. It’s the language on science not being strong enough.”
United Kingdom lead climate negotiator
Kate Hughes said the draft text “moves us backwards on the science” and does not acknowledge the urgency or scale of the climate crisis.
“It should have been instead presenting bold, collective ambition on climate action.”
Least Developed Countries group
The Least Developed Countries group said: “We struggled to find meaningful outcomes that respond to the priorities of the most vulnerable countries like us. … We cannot afford to see backsliding.”
The group is composed of 44 countries that are the most vulnerable to climate change and have contributed relatively little in carbon emissions.
They represent more than 1 billion people and include Pacific island nations, such as Tuvalu and Kiribati, as well as other countries most at risk to the effects of climate change, such as Bangladesh, Nepal and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Marshall Islands delegation
“We have been let down on all sides,” the Marshall Islands said. “We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future.”
Vanuatu delegation
The delegation for the Pacific island nation said: “This text falls short of what international law requires, what science demands and what our vulnerable communities urgently need.”
It called it “unacceptable” that the text was “silent” on fossil fuels.
Kenya delegation
Kenya’s delegation complained that the deal did not specifically mention Africa and did not take into account “Africa’s special needs and circumstances”.
“Those who took the lead in emissions cuts take the lead in support.”
Iraq delegation
The Iraq delegation expressed its “deep concern with some pathways that were taken to divert from [the] Paris Agreement”.
Russia delegation
Sergei Kononuchenko, a Russian delegate, argued that if oil and gas supplies shrink, it would lead to a “switch to dirtier types of fuel and energy poverty, … and the first to suffer would be the poorest”.
“For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel.”
Saudi Arabia delegation
The Saudi delegation said it believed “climate change requires all solutions on the table” and it made no sense for “concrete solutions” to be “taken off the table”.
COP31 president
Murat Kurum, Turkiye’s minister of environment, urbanisation and climate change, said: “We did everything we could. You should not hurt people in the world who really expect something out of this by just being hung up on one word or phrase. … There is no benefit for anyone in a system where you go into negotiations with no result.”
“There will be no new text from now on. We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus. We will implement existing decisions.”
COP31 president of negotiations
Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister of climate change and energy, called the collapse of the talks “very disappointing”.
“A lot of good things happened this COP, a lot of events which told the clean energy story, a lot of commitments made – like the more than 90 countries that signed the electrification pledge, for example. And all that is good work and a great thing but not enough when it comes to climate action,” he said.
“An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels, where some parties insisted that must be mentioned. Other parties insisted that if it was mentioned, they would veto.”

items.title: Spurs 'a match for anyone' as win at Man City boosts European hopes
items.summary:
Spurs 'a match for anyone' as European hopes boosted
- Published
Dreams of reaching the Women's Champions League may have seemed fanciful for Tottenham Hotspur when the season began.
The Women's Super League has an established big four, and big-spending London City Lionesses were the side making the
items.text:
Spurs 'a match for anyone' as European hopes boosted
- Published
Dreams of reaching the Women's Champions League may have seemed fanciful for Tottenham Hotspur when the season began.
The Women's Super League has an established big four, and big-spending London City Lionesses were the side making the most obvious play to disrupt that dominance.
But a hugely impressive and deserved win at Manchester City on Sunday afternoon proves Spurs are a team on the up, and the table shows they remain firmly in top-three contention.
Two late goals secured a 3-1 win at Joie Stadium, but this was no smash-and-grab job. Spurs were more dynamic than sluggish City, pressing them into submission.
They restricted their hosts' stellar attack to precious few chances and took the ones they created.
"When we are on our game, we can be a match for anyone," Spurs manager Martin Ho said in his post-match media conference.
"It gives us confidence - but it is just one game."
Victory kept Spurs, whose highest finish in the WSL is fifth, firmly in the mix this time.
They are fifth again, but just three points behind London City Lionesses who occupy the final European place as the league heads into a last international break of 2026.
Chelsea lead the way from Manchester City, with Manchester United one point ahead of Tottenham, who in turn sit handily clear of their sixth-placed north London rivals Arsenal.
The big four are therefore all present in the top six. London City are right there, too, and Spurs, with six wins from 11 games so far, are gamely pressing their own case.
What made Sunday's win and performance from Tottenham even more impressive is how dreadful their recent record against Manchester City had been.
Tottenham had lost six of their previous seven away matches against City in all competitions, averaging over four goals conceded per defeat.
Last season City won this fixture 5-2 with Khadija Shaw scoring a 13-minute hat-trick, the quickest in WSL history.
Shaw's early goal on Sunday, her 16th in league matches versus Spurs, could easily have started a landslide.
That was expected. City had won each of their past 17 WSL home games, including all 10 in 2026 – until Tottenham tore up the script.
The outcome means Manchester City, beaten at Chelsea in their previous outing, have suffered consecutive league losses for the first time since January 2025.
'We have maybe been naive - I own that'
Tottenham's victory came down to Ho's brave tactics and his team's superb execution of them.
After going behind, they pressed City constantly, forcing errors and creating chances. That tenacity won them countless one-on-ones, with City unable or unwilling to play over the press.
After her goal, Shaw was rendered anonymous by the hard work and close marking of centre-backs Toko Koga and Amanda Nilden.
Down the right, Kirsty Hanson dominated Carlotta Wamser, could have been awarded a penalty and provided the low cross for Cathinka Tandberg's equaliser.
In midfield, Drew Spence pulled all the strings and covered the entire pitch. At 34, she is perhaps playing the best football of her career and deserved her assist for the winner. After Matilda Vinberg put Spurs in front, several players ran to celebrate with Spence.
"When you come into this, you wonder if it will go against you, but the players were outstanding," said Ho.
"We haven't won here in so long, so we know it will be a tough game, but I have belief in my team when we are on song. I thought we were outstanding - we worked every blade of grass."
Spurs are clearly capable of taking the game to anyone in the league and have now scored 28 WSL goals this season, with only Chelsea and London City having more.
In the second half they adapted to City sending on such fluid attacking threats as Mary Fowler, Kerstin Casperij and Beth Mead.
They lifted the gas from the press, applying it more sparingly, and were solid in defence.
It shows that Ho has learned painful lessons from the past - whether from Spurs' poor record against City, including two five-goal losses in 2025-26, or conceding six to Chelsea and London City back to back in October.
"We have maybe been naive at times and I own that, so we are more reserved," Ho said of his tactical approach. "It was managing that, and the players' communication was excellent."
City were limited to fleeting chances. Jade Rose blasting over after keeper Lize Kop parried a Lauren Hemp free-kick was as close as they came to a second goal, and those were their first shots after a 50-minute drought.
When Spurs got their late chances through the hard work of Vinberg, they could strike for three points.
Vinberg had quite the rollercoaster afternoon. She was initially named on the bench but was promoted to the starting XI 15 minutes before kick-off as Olivia Holdt was suffering stomach cramps.
Perhaps unprepared, she gave away the ball playing out of defence leading to City's opener. But she grew into the game, scored Spurs' second goal and set up Jess Naz for the third.
It was a great moment for Naz, on her 100th WSL appearance of a career that has been disrupted by injury.
Spurs are back in Manchester before Christmas, visiting United on 20 December.
There will be real hope of a positive result as they press their way into contention for what would be a historic achievement of a top-three finish.
